summary: Defines an experimental protocol for sending a short message to a given user on a given terminal on a given host. It is the second version of the Message Send Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like a tiny pop-up note. You can send a short message that appears on a particular person's screen on a particular computer.

subtitle: A tiny protocol for pushing a short text message onto a specific user's terminal, over UDP or TCP port 18.

tldr.problem: Some hosts do not run Internet protocols all the time, yet people still want to send a short message to a given user on a given terminal of a given host.
tldr.mechanism: A message is a revision octet plus eight null-terminated parts (recipient, terminal, text, sender and so on), sent to port 18 over UDP or TCP, with an optional + or - acknowledgment.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental protocol that obsoletes RFC 1159. The SIGNATURE part is reserved for sender verification, but the RFC does not define its encoding.

today: RFC 1312 is an Experimental protocol that obsoletes RFC 1159, and no later RFC obsoletes it. It says the encoding of the SIGNATURE token would be left to future RFCs.

sections.title: What the Message Send Protocol Does
sections.content:
The Message Send Protocol sends a short message to a given user on a given terminal on a given host. Unix's host-local write command offers a limited form of the same service, and some hosts call it "SEND".

The motivation is that more and more people use hosts that do not run Internet protocols at all times. Such hosts can use a simple protocol built on UDP and IP. A TCP-based message sending service also exists through the SEND command of SMTP, but the RFC notes that most vendors do not implement it and that it is hard for unskilled users. For standardization, this RFC also defines a TCP-based service. This document obsoletes RFC 1159.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a way to slip a short note onto someone's screen, even if their computer is only sometimes connected to the network.

sections.title: Message Syntax
sections.content:
A message starts with one octet giving the protocol revision, currently decimal 66, the letter B. Every other part is a null-terminated sequence of eight-bit characters in the ISO 8859/1 alphabet. All parts must be present, though some may be empty, and comparisons of parts are case-insensitive.

  • RECIPIENT: the user the message is for. If empty, any user of the destination system may receive it.
  • RECIP-TERM: the terminal. If empty, the system picks the "right" one; an asterisk (the string "*") means all terminals. If both RECIPIENT and RECIP-TERM are empty, the message goes to the "console".
  • MESSAGE: the text, with lines ended by CR + LF.
  • SENDER and SENDER-TERM: who is sending, so a reply can be addressed. These were not present in version 1.
  • COOKIE: up to 32 octets, excluding the terminating null. A client may send a message several times, and the server can use the sender's UDP port plus the cookie to discard duplicates.
  • SIGNATURE: a token a server may use to verify the sender.

The whole message must be less than 512 octets, counting all eight parts and their nulls, because UDP packets are limited to 512 octets.

Message text may contain only printable ISO 8859/1 characters plus CR, LF and TAB. Clients should strip other control codes and escape sequences, and servers must check incoming messages for them. A server may display the cleaned message or reject it entirely.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is filled in like a form with boxes for who it is to, which screen, what it says and who sent it. Boxes you do not need can stay empty, and the whole form has to fit on one small card.

sections.title: The TCP and UDP Services
sections.content:
Both services use port 18. With TCP, the server listens for connections and the client sends a message over the connection. The server answers with one character, a plus sign for delivered to some user and terminal or a minus sign for not delivered to any terminal, immediately followed by an optional explanation ending in a null. Several messages may share one connection, and the client should close first.

With UDP, the server listens for datagrams and may send an answering datagram. A positive acknowledgment should be sent only if the RECIPIENT part was non-empty and the message was delivered to that user. If the message was for any user, or could not be delivered, no reply is sent.

The reason is broadcast. A UDP message might be sent to a particular user on an unknown system, or to all users on all systems, and it would be inappropriate for every server to answer.

A positive acknowledgment may only mean the server managed to invoke a local delivery service. The RFC does not say whether it means delivered to that service, displayed, or read by the user.
sections.plainLanguage: On the phone-like version, the receiver says plus for "got it" or minus for "could not give it to anyone". On the postcard-like version, the receiver stays quiet unless it delivered to the named person, so a shout to the whole street does not get a thousand replies.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC encodes a message from the user sandy at the console of system alpha to the user chris on system beta, with the terminal unknown. The text is two lines: "Hi" and "How about lunch?".

The encoding is the revision octet B, then chris, an empty RECIP-TERM, the message with a CR LF between lines, sandy, console, the cookie 910806121325 and an empty SIGNATURE, each ended by a null. The cookie is the time of day, here 12:13:25 on the 6th of August, 1991. The sending and receiving systems are not in the message; the server gets them from the transport service.
sections.plainLanguage: Sandy writes "Hi, how about lunch?" and addresses it to Chris without saying which screen. The note also carries Sandy's name and a time stamp so it can be told apart from copies.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists three issues. First, the service may write on a user's terminal without permission, so users should be given a way to disable it. Second, implementors must follow the filtering rules for message text, or they may open major security holes. This applies to any part that may be displayed, including the sender's name and terminal.

Third, the sender's identity may be faked. The service is meant for "open" environments such as controlled local area networks with reasonably trusted participants. Elsewhere, the source IP address can be spoofed. The SIGNATURE part exists so a server can reliably identify the sender. If it is empty, a server may reject the request. If it is present, it is a case-insensitive text encoding of a security token, but this RFC does not define its encoding or interpretation.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone could write on your screen or pretend to be someone else, so the rules say to strip out sneaky characters, let people turn it off, and use it only among people you trust.
